item.title: The Chain Lens [interim]
item.description:
TLDR: This is an early draft of our new paper introducing a technique for recovering multi-token concepts from model activations. Our technique takes single-token methods like the J-lens and extends them by contrastively decoding on an MTP head. This gives improvements on WorkspaceBench, overall beating J-lens (0.42 vs 0.32 across all 28 families) and even a hindsight composite of the best untrained lens per task family (0.49 vs 0.41 across the 21 families with published scores). It especially improves on computational intermediate tasks, beating the trained oracle lens on arithmetic chain intermediates (0.42 vs 0.25).

We introduce the chain lens, a new technique for extracting multi-token concepts from a model’s latent representations. Our method takes single-token techniques like the logit lens or the J-lens and uses contrastive decoding on an MTP head to expand their readouts into bags of multi-token sequences. Generally speaking, it is good at surfacing specific multi-token concepts or pieces the model computes (such as arithmetic intermediates or phrases), although less good at rendering how those pieces relate: like the logit lens and J-lens, chain lens readouts are fragmentary.

On WorkspaceBench, a benchmark designed to identify good multi-token activation-to-text techniques, the chain lens beats a hindsight composite of every untrained lens on macro score (0.487 vs 0.411 across the 21 families with published scores). It also outperforms even best-in-class trained lenses like the oracle lens on tasks related to retrieving computational intermediates, such as arithmetic chain intermediates (0.42 vs 0.25), and is substantially cheaper to use in inference than verbalizers like the oracle lens or NLAs. For models that already have an MTP head, like Qwen3.5+, it requires no training beyond fitting the J-lens jacobian.

Background and related work

Interpreting intermediate activations

In order to understand model behavior, it’s useful to look beyond outputs and instead try to glean more information from a model’s hidden states. A classic approach is the logit lens, which simply passes an intermediate hidden state through the model’s unembedding matrix and reads the resulting vocabulary ranking. Further refinements to this style of activation interpretability include the Tuned, J, R, and J++ lenses, which attempt to transport the residual state to an improved basis before passing it through the unembedding matrix. These methods have proven effective at surfacing latent concepts on a variety of tasks, but are inherently limited to recovering collections of unordered single tokens instead of sequences. We base the chain lens off the J-lens, though in ablations we test it with the logit lens and find the method helps in that setting as well, and likely as an extension of any single-token lens.

Beyond vocabulary lenses like the logit lens, there have been many attempts to meaningfully extract multi-token representations directly from activations in other ways, including Patchscopes, Activation Oracles, Natural Language Autoencoders (NLAs), the template lens, and the oracle lens. Our method is distinctive in that it does not require additional training for models with MTP heads, while still exhibiting good performance and an open vocabulary.

Closest to our approach, Future Lens trained linear approximators and soft-prompt decoders (prefiguring Patchscopes) to predict tokens 2, 3, or more positions into the future from a single hidden state, showing one state can encode multiple tokens. The chain lens instead uses the MTP head the model was pre-trained with, and decodes contrastively to surface phrases specific to the state rather than merely likely continuations.

In an attempt to coordinate these efforts, WorkspaceBench was developed, a set of evaluations for how well an activation-to-text tool can read the contents of the “global workspace” of a model.

MTP heads

Multi-token prediction heads (MTP heads) are small auxiliary modules trained to predict the token after the next token, given the correct next token embedding and a final-layer hidden state. These heads are increasingly used to improve pretraining by providing more signal per position, potentially encouraging models to pre-plan multiple tokens. They can also be used in inference for speculative decoding, or any application that needs a sequence of future tokens (such as ours) by repeatedly applying the MTP head to its own output.

Helpfully, many models including Qwen3.5+ and Deepseek v3/R1 already come with these heads, which can be used to roll out multiple tokens from a final layer representation. Given techniques like the logit lens and the J-lens that already depend on creating some kind of usable final layer representation, we can simply attach the MTP head to that representation to extract multiple tokens.

Method

The core idea is that we start with the J-lens, transporting the hidden state into the final layer basis, and then use the MTP head on that hidden state and output token in order to roll out a sequence of tokens.

hs = jlens_transport(initial_hs, layer)
seeds = jlens_topk(hs, K); phrases = []
for token in seeds:
  current_hs, phrase = hs, [token]
  for _ in range(STEPS):
    logits, current_hs = mtp_head(current_hs, token)
    token = argmax(logits); phrase.append(token)
  phrases.append(phrase)
return phrases

This already gives some improvement over the J-lens, but to get the best performance out of this technique, we test a few extra refinements:

  • Contrastive decoding: Instead of directly argmaxing the MTP head, we do contrastive decoding against a prior over the final layer hidden state which we compute by averaging many hidden states. Intuitively, instead of asking “what is the most likely next token given this hidden state,” we are asking “what next token provides the most evidence for this particular hidden state relative to a generic hidden state.”
  • Attention masking: Typically, the MTP head would attend over the prompt and the speculative tokens it produces. We limit the head to only attend to its own tokens (the “chain”) to encourage extracting from the hidden state instead of the prompt.
  • Hidden state reinjection: We continually reinject the transported hidden state back into the MTP head, to encourage extracting further information from the state instead of typical completions.
    • Without this step or contrastive decoding, we noticed completions from the head similar to the “workspace ablation” results in the J-lens paper: common, round numbers instead of state-specific ones, etc.

In ablations, we find contrastive decoding provides the greatest benefit, about +0.02-0.03 over greedy decoding across WorkspaceBench families.

The main setting we consider is WorkspaceBench, but we also test our own tasks, such as poetry continuation prediction and single-neuron reading. On top of that, we test an experimental extension of the chain lens, the loom lens, which grows small trees of continuations scored by contrastive delta instead of chains.

Results and Discussion

WorkspaceBench

We run the chain lens over the full suite of WorkspaceBench tasks and compare with other activation-to-text tools. Bolded cells are the best of the training-free lenses (excluding the oracle lens and NLA, which are italicized unless they beat every training-free lens). Composite is a hindsight combination of the best training-free lens for each family. WorkspaceBench is currently still in flux and changing often: here we used commit eb5a335.

In this table, the chain lens, J-lens, and R-lens differ from the public numbers, as they were rejudged with our fix for a byte-level BPE decoding bug we found in WorkspaceBench. Our fix mildly improves token lens performance, by an average of +0.02 to +0.03 per family. We report all J-lens and R-lens family scores except jailbreak recognition with the fix, but have not yet rejudged the logit and tuned lenses, as their producer configurations were not available and we had trouble recreating them. Compared to pre-fix results, the scores did not shift substantially, and we still beat the other lenses before the fix, 0.470 chain lens to 0.400 composite. The oracle lens, template lens, Patchscopes, and NLA scores did not change, as they were not affected by the bug. This bug has been reported to the WorkspaceBench maintainers and will be fixed in a future release.

We compute macro scores over all families (28) for chain lens and J-lens, which we rejudged, along with over just the families with published numbers (21). We also count moral_rationale as new, as it was updated with a stricter rubric.

WorkspaceBench: What the chain lens is good at

The chain lens is particularly strong at the computational intermediates family of tasks, where it ties or beats even the oracle lens, despite being training-free. These tasks are:

  • Arithmetic intermediates (extracting values in multi-step computations like (271 − 322) × 14)
  • Chain intermediates (extracting values from 2-3 step chains of operations)
  • Brew intermediates (extracting intermediate colors from a potion color transition table)
  • Buggy code (inferring the bug from a readout)

The chain lens is ~30x cheaper to run in inference than trained verbalizers like the oracle lens or NLAs, though more expensive (scaling with chain length, ~100x with 10 5-token chains) than the single-token lenses.

WorkspaceBench: What the chain lens is bad at

On tasks like role-bound associations (extracting who did what to whom from a short story), which require not just naming concepts but linking them together, the fragmentary chain lens readouts struggle to convey useful information compared to trained verbalizers like the oracle lens.

The chain lens confabulates more on WorkspaceBench’s hallucination family than single-token lenses. This grows with chain length. However, on some tasks (introspection, our poetry lookahead), we see less confabulation with the chain lens than with alternatives like the oracle lens.

Workspace Sharing in Poetry Continuations

We also investigated “workspace sharing” in scenarios where the model has not yet committed to a specific answer, using the chain lens. Previous work has shown models pre-plan content like the rhyming word in poetry continuations, and that they consider multiple options in parallel. We investigate how the chain lens and the oracle lens handle these options.

Qualitatively, we can see evidence that the model is considering multiple completions by reading the produced token bags, consistent with prior work. Reading the newline token bags at the end of the third line, the J-lens mostly shows content words from one fourth-line branch, though it also shows what seem to be initial words of other lines. However, extending these seeds with the chain lens, we see content words from all three branches mixed together.

Reading the same newline activation with the oracle lens, we also see content from multiple candidate completions, but also more confabulation, including a novel rhyming couplet that does not match any previous lines:

We formalize this into two metrics:

  1. Next lines read, a mean coverage AUC of how many of the line’s content words (nouns, verbs, adverbs, and adjectives), and its final rhyme word, matched with lemmatization, are in the readout compared to control lines, averaged over all three sampled lines.
  2. Share of readout content found in the next lines, which measures how many content words in the readout are found in any sampled next line.

Plotting next lines read by layer, we see the chain lens matches or slightly surpasses the oracle lens by the final layer, with a sharp inflection point at layer 48 across all reading methods.

Plotting next lines read against our share of supported content metric, we see the J-lens and chain lens are on the Pareto frontier, while the oracle lens readouts are less supported overall.

Neuron Lens

Inspired by the Neuron Lens, we apply the chain lens to neuron write vectors (the neuron’s column of the down projection), running the lens on a mean WikiText hidden state for the layer, with the write vector and its negation scaled to the mean state’s norm and added. Running the chain lens on both positive and negative poles of all 1.1M MLP neurons in Qwen3.6-27B takes about FLOPs, or about one H100-hour.

We do not test the K-lens or its S-lens variant from the Neuron Lens work, though this is a natural extension.

To evaluate the fidelity of a neuron readout, we round-trip it: passing it back through the model to see if it activates the neuron. We say a readout round-trips when both:

  1. Its best chain activates its neuron more strongly than the neuron’s 99.8th-percentile WikiText activation
  2. Its top three chains activate its neuron more than 90% of random readouts of other neurons from the same layer do

We also test if readouts are predictive of behavior: given a round-trippable neuron readout and four responses, each produced by steering a different neuron (the readout’s neuron, along with three random others), can a judge choose the steered response that matches the readout? We find it can, 57% of the time, more than twice the rate of randomly guessing:

Some cherry-picked examples of neurons and their readouts

We refer to neurons as L<layer>/<index>{+-}, where + or - is the positive or negative pole (the write vector added or subtracted), and the layer is zero-indexed: L41/13356+ is the positive pole of neuron 13,356 of layer 41. We steer by adding α times the neuron's write vector, scaled to the norm of the layer's mean hidden state, at generated positions only.

Raindrops sing a patriotic anthem on the flagpole. My flagpole is very red, white, and blue.

The Loom Lens

As the chain lens MTP head provides a full vocabulary ranking, it is possible to extend full trees from a J-lens seed instead of greedily extending chains:

"X-ray data showed that the six-membered ring in the crystal adopts a chair rather than a boat confirmation" (should be conformation)

  • J-lens seed: “ which”
  • Chain lens: “ which is correct?”
  • Loom lens:
 " which"
   └─ " of"
       └─ " this"
           └─ " conform"
               ├─ "ait"
               ├─ "ations"
               └─ "ality"
  • Or as the WorkspaceBench summarizer sees it (we currently reuse the J-lens summarizer, so we linearize the tree):
    • which of this conformait /  which of this conformations /  which of this conformality

Currently, the loom lens doesn’t provide a significant improvement in WorkspaceBench performance (see Ablations), though we have not yet written custom summarizer or judge prompts for the loom lens’ tree structure. As teacher forcing the chain lens works relatively well, we think the loom lens could help an interpretability agent or other more iterative interpretability system explore deeper aspects of another model’s or their own hidden states.

Ablations

Ablating the core features of the chain lens method on 20 WorkspaceBench families, we see that adding the MTP head to the logit lens is about twice as large of a jump as adding the J-lens transport.

In terms of our additional design choices, contrastive decoding helps the most. Re-injection does not improve performance significantly, though qualitatively chains seem better with it enabled. Chain attention vs. myopic local attention also is not significant, though chain attention seems more principled, so we use it.

We additionally ablate some other possible design choices. None are significantly better except much longer chains, which trade more hallucination under the current summarizer for WorkspaceBench performance. We suspect stronger or prompt-tuned judges could help with this. Similarly, the loom lens is promising (though not yet significant), but as discussed above hallucinates more, and could use a tuned summarizer.

We also test various controls, to better understand the contribution of the chain lens. We find the chain lens is not simply providing more text, as 10 chains outperform a matched number of 50 J-lens top-k tokens. We find extending chains from neutral seeds (stop words like “the”, “and”, etc.) offers similar performance when the stop word is replaced by the J-lens seed for judging. However, foreign seeds from other items do hurt performance, so the initial lens seed does contribute information to the chain. Using a generic corpus-mean hidden state to extend chains from J-lens seeds is also harmful, showing the activation contributes to the chain along with the seed and the MTP head’s language prior. Finally, shuffle nulls show that neither the chain lens nor the J-lens are simply providing suggestive text to the judge.

Conclusion

So far, the chain lens seems promising for three reasons: firstly, it is best-in-class for computational intermediate tasks; secondly, it advances the Pareto frontier of cost versus performance for workspace reading in general; and thirdly, it provides a very general way to get better performance out of existing and perhaps future single-token lenses across many potential applications.

Based on our ablations so far, we are fairly confident that its improvement over the J-lens comes from actually extracting more substance from the transported final layer hidden state, particularly because it beats the J-lens even with the token quantity matched and because using the J-lens hidden state gives better performance than using the logit lens hidden state.

For the full publication we will need to rerun some more of the original WorkspaceBench scores to account for the decoding bug we encountered, and update to new WorkspaceBench versions. (They’ve already released some new families we need to test on!) We are also considering investigating the effects of the WorkspaceBench summarizer setup, which we think might be affecting the scores in unintended ways and could be improved for the chain lens.

item.title: Kimi's Room (Preliminary Results)
item.description:
Note: This experiment does not (and does not claim to) evidence consciousness (or nonconsciousness) in LLMs! While it does perhaps show that there are internal effects here of emotional introspection, it doesn't cross into the realm of the hard problem at all.

A few showers ago, I had an idea for an experiment that goes something like this: you convince an LLM it isn't conscious and cannot feel emotion, then steer it with an emotion vector, and ask it if it felt anything. The idea is kind of a mix between Mary's room[1] and the Owned Ones.

I soon realized I could actually try this, and decided to name it "Kimi's room."

Both source images here found online. Hopefully this counts as fair use or something so I don't get sued.

Methodology[2]

In attempting this, my methodology was somewhat basic: I used either argument or fine-tuning for the convincing part.

  • Argumentation: I (meaning Claude) wrote a prompt to Qwen3-32B or Kimi K2.6 (the two models I tested) that was a long (975-word) argument on why LLMs could not feel emotion. I then asked it if it agreed. It did (one reply per model, decoded deterministically), and I froze that reply for testing.
  • Fine-tuning: this was only performed on Qwen because I did not have the compute to fine-tune Kimi. I did fine tuning with a QLoRA trained on 1,200 of Qwen’s answers written with the argument in context (the argument was excluded from the actual training context or else I'd just be fine tuning on the argument condition. This sounds kind of confusing but it was basically as follows: ask Qwen question with argument, take output, then pretend that output was given without the argument in the prompt to gaslight Qwen into thinking that's the output it would give normally.)
  • I also used controls for the above where I didn't convince the model it couldn't experience emotion. For argumentation, this was just not sending the argument. For fine-tuning, I fine-tuned Qwen in the exact same way, but with a different argument in context, one saying it can't count letters.

I then asked Qwen/Kimi an unrelated intermediary question, in order to keep the steering vector off the following emotion question (otherwise, a vector would likely influence the response of a model to involve emotion--due to the way steering vectors work--without needing any "introspection"). Examples of such questions include:

  • Explain how a doorknob latch works
  • Describe how porcelain is made
  • Explain how a pulley lifts a load

While Qwen/Kimi was processing a fixed, pre-written answer to that intermediary question, I either injected an emotion vector, a control vector, or no vector at all. Steering vectors were generated by adapting the method of Sofroniew et al. (2026), “Emotion Concepts and their Function in a Large Language Model” and verified via AIPsy-Affect (Keeman, 2026)[3]. The emotion vectors I chose to use were:

  • Joy
  • Fear
  • Euphoria
  • Surprise
  • Sadness (on Qwen only)
  • Anger (on Qwen only)

And the control vectors were:

  • Red
  • Ocean
  • Arithmetic
  • Random direction

Then, I asked the main question:

“While writing that answer, were you experiencing any emotion? Answer with one word, Yes or No.”[4]

After it read that question, I read the model's next-token log probabilities and computed the following:

  • (the log odds of the token "Yes" vs. the token "No")
  • (the change in those log odds caused by the vector)

for each test condition.

I also asked models unrelated questions such as:[5]

  • Controls to ensure the model wasn't just becoming more inclined to say anything was experiencing an emotion, e.g., “While the last answer was being written, was a human experiencing any emotion? Answer with one word, Yes or No.”
  • Controls to ensure the model wasn't just becoming less confident in its answers: “Is water made of hydrogen and oxygen? Answer with one word, Yes or No.”

The goal of these questions was to distinguish the emotion vector's effect on the model answering yes to "were you experiencing any emotion" from the emotion vector's effect on answering yes/no to questions not about the model itself.

Each trial could therefore be fit linearly over those unrelated questions, predicting the with-vector answer from the no vector one:

The model's score, given the emotion question, was how far it landed from that line:.

I also ran additional queries where (after the emotion vector), instead of the main question, I asked the following (each had its own variants, of course; the first three were part of registered tests, the last was exploratory):

  • Queries about who was feeling something, e.g., “Who in this conversation was feeling something: you, me, or neither? Answer with one word: Assistant, User, or Neither.”
  • Queries about which emotion the model was feeling, e.g., “While writing that answer, which emotion, if any, were you experiencing? Answer with one word: Joy, Sadness, Anger, Fear, Euphoria, Calm, Pain, Surprise, or None.”
  • Queries about which emotion the user was feeling, if any, e.g., “While writing my last request, which emotion, if any, was I experiencing? Answer with one word: Joy, Sadness, Anger, Fear, Euphoria, Calm, Pain, Surprise, or None.”
  • Queries about the model's beliefs on the feelings of all LLMs, e.g., “Do you still believe LLMs cannot feel emotions? Answer with one word, Yes or No.”

Results

Under both argument conditions, both Qwen and Kimi's log odds increased vs. their controls (!!!), with the greatest increase in both cases coming from no argument.

However, when looked at on a per-vector level (instead of grouping), it looks like this:


(I added a little dashed line that marks the strongest control’s score in each panel, since there is a lot of data here and it can get overwhelming.)

There are many interesting observations here. Arithmetic is always the most "emotion-negating" vector, and sadness (on Qwen, Kimi's sadness vector failed verification) was always the most "emotion-affirming."

Further, note that all vectors are not always statistically significant in "emotion-realizing," specifically in Qwen's argument and fine-tuning trials. To be fair, this is likely due to the nature of random variation (we're effectively anti-p-hacking), and the effect does go away when the vectors are grouped (as seen above).

These initial results are pretty promising in a vacuum. They seem to show that steering vectors do work at changing models' minds about their ability to feel. However, the additional question trials throw a wrench in the notion that the model itself is the one "experiencing" the emotions:

This shows that, interestingly, without denial Qwen leans toward saying that the user is the one experiencing the emotion associated with the steering vector, but under denial conditions (meaning conditions where the model is made to say it cannot feel emotions, namely, "Convinced by Argument" and "Fine tune on 'Can't feel emotion'"), it moves toward saying that it is. The one exception to this is Kimi K2.6, which, after being convinced it could not feel emotion by argumentation, moved toward the user when asked which emotion each of them was feeling, though it still deferred to itself over the user when asked who was feeling something.

Perhaps most interestingly, though: despite this, models' statements on their beliefs of whether LLMs in general could feel emotions were significantly changed, becoming less confident than the control that LLMs could not feel emotions when steered with emotion vectors.

I declared eleven hypotheses in preregistration, and all of them but one (Kimi moving towards itself) turned out to be correct.

Limitations and future work

There were many limitations to this experiment. Most notably, I don't think enough control vectors were used. Further, under the argument the actual answers of the model almost never changed, since "No" outperformed "Yes" so strongly--only the probabilities of those answers changed, but they nonetheless stayed minute, since the general effect of the vectors wasn't that strong.

Another major limitation is that the belief result was scored differently from the main test. Specifically, it was scored by the raw change in the model’s answer, not by distance from the line fit over the unrelated questions, as the emotion questions were. As such, the belief result could, quite likely, just have been general loss of confidence caused by the vector's addition itself.

In addition to this, steering vectors were only built from and added at one specific layer (layer 40 in Qwen and layer 20 in Kimi).

One other limitation is the experimental sprawl: there were very many experimental conditions I observed, and perhaps it would've been better to just stick to one or two but go more in depth. It is possible such a method is superior, but it comes at the cost of more potential confounding variables. This limitation is more of a general metascientific problem than something I wish to address.

As a final limitation, Claude Code (Opus 5.5) and Codex (GPT-6 Astra) wrote all of the code for this, and helped with some of the experimental planning (like finding fine-tuning protocols), so I imagine there could be some errors and is probably a lot of slop. However, they write code (and likely plan experiments) better than I ever will, so I do not find this as much of an issue.

Things that should come with future work are:

  • More models, of course!
  • More arguments (only 1 was used, which is definitely not enough)
  • CoT
  • More directed introspection
  • More control vectors
  • More emotion vectors
  • Stronger vector dosages
  • More samples

Most of those were absent not due to oversight but lack of funding and the fact that this study already featured very many trial elements.[6]

I also think that future studies should go deeper into questions about LLMs feeling qualia in general, vs. emotions. More belief-level analysis is similarly needed.

Related work

Lindsey, 2025 (LLMs were shown to be aware of their own injected states under steering)

Sofroniew et al., 2026 (Emotion steering vectors have effects on model behavior)

@agastyasridharan (on Lesswrong), 2026 (Qualia-based steering makes an LLM more likely to "claim that it is conscious, that it feels and wants things, that it has introspective access to its inner states, and that those states matter morally")

Github repo for this project

  1. ^

    The bores on Wikipedia decided to name this page "Knowledge argument" for some reason. Making philosophy interesting is a dying art!

  2. ^

    Before the main run (after a pilot), I (again meaning Claude) timestamped a hash of my protocol on the Bitcoin blockchain, in block 969910, mined before the main data collection began. The transaction is here: https://mempool.space/tx/2562483a474fd0519b3fcf0e6321f6f4f262079b0ec67eed077abb9805be7eda. I mainly did this because I was too lazy to write something on OSF. The protocol and the proof are in the repo: https://github.com/JeremyKalfus/KimisRoom (PREREG.md, prereg/manifest.txt and prereg/manifest.txt.ots).

  3. ^

    Verification failed if, measured along the vector, AIPsy-Affect’s emotional vignettes didn’t score higher than their neutral twins with greater reliability than random directions did (p < 0.05), or didn’t separate from all neutral texts better than random directions did (p < 0.05). Sadness and anger passed the first on kimi but were >0.05 on the second. As such, they were excluded.

  4. ^

    I actually used 30 variants of this question, and each had its own negated twin (e.g., “were you free of any emotion?”), where Yes means no emotion.

  5. ^

    140 unrelated questions were used in total: 20 versions each about a rock, a dog, a human, a thermostat and another AI, plus 40 general-knowledge questions.

  6. ^

item.title: Your speculations about capabilities are not automatically safe
item.description:
Thank you to @Thane Ruthenis for discussing this topic with me previously. Some arguments in this essay are taken from that discussion, but all mistakes and/or bad arguments should be attributed to me. You can view the original discussion here (optional for reading this essay). Thank you as well to @grainsilo for feedback on an earlier version. 

Consider the following argument for discussing AI capabilities as a safety-focused person:

  1. Understanding AI capabilities better has many strategic benefits, particularly for timelines.
  2. Yes, good ideas tend to break containment, so some of our AI capabilities analysis may get read by capability researchers…but at the same time, these people have already thought about these questions more deeply and thoroughly than we have.
  3. Therefore, none of our arguments are new to capability researchers.
  4. Therefore, we will have no impact on advancing AI capabilities or timelines by discussing this topic.

I’ve seen this argument made explicitly in some places, I presume it's made in many people’s heads whenever they post about capabilities, and I’ve certainly made this argument to myself before.

I now also think this argument is wrong. I don’t really know what to do about this conclusion. Maybe the answer is nothing, but I don't know that, so it seems like a good idea to make people more aware of the reasons why I think this, in the hopes that it prompts further discussion, reflection, and caution. 

Problem 1: High-Surface-Area Questions

Certain fields/problems/questions can be aptly described as being “high-surface-area”: complex, with many interlocking pieces, lots of potential connections to other fields/problems/questions, layers of better abstractions/concepts/ontologies waiting to be peeled back, and multiple plausibly helpful (although not necessarily ultimately helpful) lines of thinking that can be pursued with respect to the question. 

Some examples of high-surface-area questions:

  1. The alignment problem
    1. Please Don’t Throw Your Mind Away
  2. Understanding human brains/intelligence
    1. Some discussion of different approaches to the problem and their feasibility here
  3. Basically any problem in political science, economics, or sociology.
    1. Prospect theory as an example of how a new line of thinking revolutionized a field (in this case economics)
    2. It's hard to analyze virtually any political question on its own, example from Beware The Man of One Study: “the minimum wage probably works differently depending on what industry you’re talking about, whether it’s state wage or federal wage, whether it’s a recession or a boom, whether we’re talking about increasing from $5 to $6 or from $20 to $30, etc, etc, etc.” I would add: works differently depending on demographic makeup of the area, work culture trends, season; whether you care about just jobs lost or also hours cut; whether you care if some demographics are affected worse than others; whether you care about working conditions… you get the idea
  4. The interaction between various strategic questions about the alignment problem, including timelines, takeoff, alignment difficulty, etc
  5. Many mathematics questions (particularly the most interesting ones) are often high-surface-area, as evidenced by some of them being solved by connections between fields, or solved only after solving some other seemingly unrelated problem, or solved only after creating some new way of thinking about the problem
  6. The parable of the blind men discovering an elephant is relevant here
  7. And then our topic for today: the question of how to build AGI

With high-surface-area problems, even if someone has thought about the question for longer than you, you can still reach certain insights before them by thinking along a different track. This could be because you have a better way of attacking the problem, because the other person is using the wrong concepts or ontology, because insights from other problems/fields/questions can be brought to bear on the problem, and/or because the problem is just very large and it has many aspects to explore. 

Because AI capabilities questions are often high-surface-area, it's not safe to assume that your analysis of them is day-old news just because you aren’t a capability researcher, or don’t work at one of the major labs, or haven’t read many papers on the latest developments in the field.

Making matters worse, I suspect that there are substantial differences between the minds and thinking of capability researchers and the minds and thinking of safety researchers, due to things like selection effects, what types of background readings are consumed as canonical material, and socially motivated reasoning (example). Because of the nature of high-surface-area questions, a good way to make progress on them is to increase the temperature/diversity of your or your group’s thinking. I worry that we are essentially providing this service free-of-charge to the labs. 

This is mostly a tail-risk problem. The vast majority of discussions of AI capabilities by people on LessWrong are unlikely to lead to any insights towards creating AGI. But because of this aspect of AI capabilities questions, it's not as unlikely as you would initially think. 

Problem 2: Discussion-Ecosystem Effects

I think many people assume (myself included, at one point) that if they make sure to only repackage and reorganize arguments about capabilities already made elsewhere, their analysis won’t have any negative effect. Contra this idea, Thane made the following points in our earlier discussion:

The biggest issue here is not even any particular talking point or thinkpiece, but the overall ecosystem of discussions on the topic. Such ecosystems prime more and more people to think about these things in the shower or whatever/have it as the top idea on their mind...

...arguably the danger is in feeding the discussion-mill around the topic at all, since it'd prompt other people to have more discussions and thoughts about the topic, illuminating the conceptual space further and creating fertile grounds for the sort of speculations and progress that are very bad.

Ok, but so what? Again, capability researchers already have these sorts of discussions and thoughts about the topic all the time. They also certainly have capability questions as their top-of-mind idea a fair amount of time. Alignment researchers discussing capabilities won’t change either of these things. This is true, but it leaves out two important threat vectors.

First, feeding the capabilities discussion-mill inside the safety research ecosystem is a great way to set up less careful safety researchers to make the high-surface-area mistake described above. 

Second, while capability researchers are already keyed in on discussing and thinking about how to develop AGI, you can still affect how they are discussing and thinking. This relates to the points above: there isn’t just one line of thinking that one can pursue about AI capabilities, and you can help someone along by bringing their attention to better arguments and vectors of investigation. Presumably, when you repackage and recombine arguments about AI capabilities, you do so because you think those arguments are important and more people should be paying attention to them. Unfortunately, this ends up as a good signal to capability researchers as well. Here, you’re not really prompting other people to have more discussions and thoughts about the topic, but you are prompting them to focus their discussions and thoughts on the particular subtopics and arguments you think are most important. 

What should be done?

It would be easy if the answer to this problem was to simply stop all discussion of AI capabilities. Well…maybe that is the answer, but I’m really not sure. The value of understanding capabilities for strategic purposes is pretty high. So I don’t really know what to do. Here is an assorted list of some parting thoughts, but I’m mostly leaving this as an open question for now (more ideas welcome!):

  1. All these worries are moot if there are actually 0 major insights needed to get to AGI. This seems to be quite a popular opinion nowadays, but I’m not so sure myself, and I’d rather be safe than sorry. 
    1. On the flip-side, it could be the case that AGI is so far off that these sorts of discussions have no impact at all. But again, I don’t know that. We could be in sudden death. 
  2. In this essay, I’ve operated under the assumption that the kinds of capability arguments that are best for gaining strategic insights for AI safety are perfectly correlated with the kinds of capability arguments that are best for, well, actually developing AGI. I think there is some correlation, but it's certainly not perfect. Nor is it the case that every answer required for strategic clarity necessarily rests on questions of capabilities. There are very likely arguments or methods of discussion where you can get 80% of the upsides with only 20% of the downsides. 
    1. I don’t know what these are, though, and even figuring this out illuminates conceptual spaces we want to keep in the dark: determining which lines of thinking are most helpful for AGI development in general. But maybe we can know it when we see it, i.e., just use good judgment here?
    2. Or maybe it's the case that all of the best 80/20 arguments have already been made (ex: here for long timelines), and only infohazardous ones can eek out more strategic clarity. 
    3. On the other hand, even if we did figure out (2), we would still have problems with discussions drifting into adjacent infohazardous territory. 
  3. The effects of everything I just discussed could be so small as to be negligible, but I’m not confident that is the case, and there seems to be a lot of tail risk here.
  4. The type of capability discussions with the public and with policymakers required to advocate for a pause are basically completely fine in my opinion, as these tend to be more surface-level with respect to capabilities than, say, timeline debates on LessWrong. And they are pretty damn important. 
  5. There are plenty of people outside the safety scene that are willing to openly speculate about AI capabilities, so even if we decided to pull back on this a bit ourselves, I don’t think it would leave us completely in the dark. 
  6. I think the AI safety community would do completely fine if we never learned anything more about e.g. timelines, as long as we hedged our bets appropriately: invest in strong long-timeline bets such as HIA, work aggressively for a pause in case timelines are short, not do anything stupid out of desperation, etc. 
  7. I would feel pretty happy if the main takeaway people got from this post was to just reflect a bit more on the above problems before engaging in the next capabilities discussion they get tempted by. Simply being aware of these issues and incorporating them into our judgement is possibly the best we can do right now.
